subject: Geography
description: Concept pool for UPSC Prelims — Geography > Physical Geography > Natural Disasters. Covers earthquakes, cyclones, floods, droughts, landslides, tsunamis, and disaster management frameworks as tested in UPSC Prelims 2014–2024. Each concept carries priority (frequency in papers), tested_as_question_types, sub_concepts (specific testable facts with aspects and linkages), links_to (intra-domain cross-concept linkages for hard A/R questions), and interlink_domains (cross-subject domain linkages).
core_concepts: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction
Avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)

sub_concepts.topic: Seismic waves — P-waves (compressional, travel through all media, arrive first) vs S-waves (shear, transverse, travel only through solids, cause more surface damage)
India's seismic zones — Zone II (least hazard) to Zone V (highest hazard); Northeast India, Himalayan belt, and Andaman-Nicobar in Zone V
Richter scale vs Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw) — Richter measures amplitude of seismic waves, Mw measures total energy released; modern seismology uses Mw for large earthquakes
Focus (hypocenter) vs epicenter — focus is underground point of rupture, epicenter is point on surface directly above focus; shallow focus earthquakes cause more surface damage
Liquefaction — waterlogged loose sediments lose shear strength during earthquake shaking, behaving like liquid; coastal and deltaic areas most vulnerable
Aftershocks vs foreshocks — foreshocks precede main quake (difficult to identify in real time), aftershocks follow; aftershock sequence can last months
Cyclone formation conditions — SST ≥26–27°C, low vertical wind shear, presence of Coriolis force (absent within 5° latitude of equator), high humidity in troposphere
IMD cyclone intensity classification — Depression, Deep Depression, Cyclonic Storm, Severe CS, Very Severe CS, Extremely Severe CS, Super Cyclonic Storm; Saffir-Simpson (US) scale is different

Bay of Bengal vs Arabian Sea cyclones — Bay of Bengal generates ~80% of Indian cyclones due to warmer SST, lower salinity, weaker Coriolis deflection; Arabian Sea cyclones are fewer but intensifying with climate change
Cyclone eye and eyewall — calm low-pressure center (eye), most violent winds in eyewall; storm surge (not wind) is the primary cause of death in coastal cyclones
India's cyclone-prone coasts — East coast (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu) more vulnerable than west coast; Odisha most frequently affected state

Types of floods — riverine (slow-rise, long-duration), flash flood (rapid onset, high velocity), coastal (storm surge, tsunami), urban (stormwater drainage failure); distinct triggers and management approaches
India's flood-prone zones — Brahmaputra and Ganga floodplains most affected; 40 million hectares flood-prone; Assam, Bihar, UP, West Bengal chronically vulnerable
Flood management structures — embankments vs dams vs wetland restoration; embankments can increase downstream flood risk; National Water Policy 2012 emphasizes non-structural measures
Floodplain zoning and 100-year flood concept — 100-year flood has 1% probability of occurring in any given year (not once in 100 years); zoning restricts development in high-risk zones
Integrated Flood Management (IFM) — combines structural and non-structural measures; promotes flood risk management over flood control; WMO/GWP framework

sub_concepts.topic: Types of mass movements — creep (slow, imperceptible), flow (debris/mudflow), slide (rotational/translational), fall (rockfall); classified by material type and velocity
linked_to: Avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)

sub_concepts.topic: Primary triggers in Indian context — rainfall is the dominant trigger (>70% of landslides in Himalayas and Western Ghats); earthquakes are secondary trigger; deforestation and road-cutting increase susceptibility
Landslide-prone zones in India — Himalayan belt (Uttarakhand, HP, J&K, NE India), Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka), Nilgiris; Geological Survey of India (GSI) maintains national landslide atlas
linked_to: Avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)

sub_concepts.topic: Debris flow vs mudslide — debris flow is mixture of rock fragments, soil, and water (faster, more destructive); mudslide is finer sediment-dominated (slower, thixotropic behavior)

Dam-induced landslide hazard — reservoir impoundment changes pore water pressure in adjacent slopes; Tehri Dam area and Koyna reservoir (1967 Koyna earthquake, M6.3) are Indian examples of reservoir-induced seismicity

links_to: Avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)

sub_concepts.topic: Drought classification — meteorological (rainfall deficiency ≥25% below normal), hydrological (reduced stream/reservoir levels), agricultural (soil moisture inadequate for crops), socio-economic (when drought impacts human welfare)
IMD drought definition — meteorological drought declared when annual rainfall deficiency ≥25%; severe drought when ≥50% deficiency; 'drought' and 'scarcity' are distinct administrative categories

El Niño and Indian drought — El Niño weakens Indian Ocean warm pool, suppresses monsoon convection, increases drought probability; relationship is probabilistic (not deterministic); ~50% of El Niño years see deficient Indian monsoon
Drought-prone regions of India — Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat, Marathwada and Vidarbha (Maharashtra), Telangana, interior Karnataka, Bundelkhand; Rajasthan chronically affected
National Drought Management Policy and PMFBY — Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (2016) as drought risk transfer mechanism; National Contingency Crop Plan for agriculture adaptation
linked_to: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

sub_concepts.topic: Tsunami generation mechanism — requires underwater earthquake WITH vertical seafloor displacement; horizontal fault movement or strike-slip faults do NOT typically generate tsunamis; also generated by submarine landslides and volcanic eruptions
Tsunami wave characteristics — long wavelength (100–1000 km), low amplitude in open ocean (<1 m), high wave speed (~700–900 km/h); amplitude increases dramatically as water shallows (shoaling effect)
Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System (IOTWS) — established after 2004 Sumatra earthquake-tsunami (M9.1); India's INCOIS (Hyderabad) is the regional tsunami warning center for Indian Ocean
Andaman-Nicobar Islands — most tsunami-vulnerable Indian territory; located close to Sunda subduction zone; 2004 tsunami killed 10,000+ in Andaman-Nicobar

Tsunami vs storm surge — tsunami is seismically generated, wave period in minutes, arrives as series of waves; storm surge is meteorologically generated, driven by cyclone low pressure and wind, single prolonged inundation
Volcanic hazards — lava flows, pyroclastic flows (fastest and most lethal), volcanic ash, lahars (volcanic mudflows), toxic gas emissions (SO2, CO2, H2S)
India's only active volcano — Barren Island (Andaman Sea, Bay of Bengal); Narcondam Island is dormant; both in Andaman-Nicobar; Barren Island last major eruption 2017–2018
Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) — logarithmic scale 0–8; VEI 8 is ultra-Plinian (supervolcano); Krakatoa 1883 was VEI 6; Pinatubo 1991 was VEI 6, caused global cooling of ~0.5°C
Ring of Fire — Pacific Ocean basin perimeter; 90% of world's earthquakes and 75% of active volcanoes; India is NOT in the Ring of Fire (Indian plate boundary lies in Himalaya and Andaman arc)
Deccan Traps — ancient flood basalts from volcanic eruptions ~66 million years ago; associated with mass extinction at K-Pg boundary; not tectonically active today

IMD heat wave definition — plains: maximum temperature ≥40°C AND departure ≥4.5°C above normal; OR maximum temperature ≥45°C regardless of departure; coastal stations: ≥37°C AND departure ≥4.5°C; hills: ≥30°C AND departure ≥4.5°C
Severe heat wave — departure ≥6.4°C above normal OR temperature ≥47°C on plains; heat wave declared over region if conditions persist for 2+ consecutive days
IMD cold wave definition — minimum temperature ≤10°C on plains AND departure ≥4.5°C below normal; severe cold wave: departure ≥6.4°C below normal
Heat stress and urban heat island effect — urban areas 2–5°C warmer than surroundings; dark surfaces, lack of vegetation, waste heat amplify heat wave impact in cities
National Action Plan on Heat — Heat Action Plans mandated for cities after 2010 Ahmedabad heat wave (1300+ deaths); Ahmedabad HAP was India's first; WHO guidance on cooling centers and early warning

sub_concepts.topic: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) — apex body under Disaster Management Act 2005; chaired by Prime Minister; issues guidelines, approves National Disaster Management Plan; NOT an operational response force
linked_to: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

sub_concepts.topic: National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) — operational arm for rescue and relief; under NDMA; 16 battalions drawn from paramilitary forces (CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, SSB); DG NDRF reports to NDMA

State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) — state-level body chaired by Chief Minister; district-level DDMA chaired by Collector/District Magistrate; hierarchical structure mirrors NDMA at state/district levels
linked_to: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

sub_concepts.topic: National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) vs State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) — NDRF supplements SDRF when state resources are inadequate; SDRF is primary fund for disaster relief; both constituted under DM Act 2005
National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP) 2016 — India's first national plan; aligned with Sendai Framework 2015–2030 targets; covers all hazard types; revised 2019
linked_to: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

sub_concepts.topic: Sendai Framework 2015–2030 — adopted March 2015 in Sendai, Japan; successor to Hyogo Framework for Action (HFA) 2005–2015; 4 priorities, 7 global targets; first global DRR framework with outcome goal
Sendai's 4 priorities — (1) Understanding disaster risk, (2) Strengthening disaster risk governance, (3) Investing in DRR for resilience, (4) Enhancing disaster preparedness for effective response

Sendai 7 global targets — reduce mortality, reduce affected people, reduce economic losses, reduce damage to critical infrastructure, increase national/local strategies, international cooperation, availability of early warning systems; targets measured against 2005–2015 baseline

Hyogo Framework vs Sendai Framework — HFA 2005–2015: 5 priorities, no quantified targets, no explicit economic loss goal; Sendai 2015–2030: 4 priorities, 7 measurable targets, explicit outcome (reduce disaster risk and losses)
SFDRR role of UNDRR — UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (formerly UNISDR) is the custodian; Sendai is non-binding (voluntary commitment); monitoring through Sendai Monitor platform

Lightning formation mechanism — charge separation in cumulonimbus clouds; ice crystals (positive charge) rise, graupel (heavy ice, negative charge) sinks; lightning discharges potential difference between cloud and ground or within cloud
Cloud-to-ground vs intra-cloud lightning — intra-cloud (sheet lightning) is most common (~75%); cloud-to-ground is most dangerous to humans; cloud-to-cloud lightning also occurs

Path of least resistance myth — lightning does NOT always strike the tallest object; it follows the ionized path of least electrical resistance (stepped leader); tall objects increase probability but do not guarantee strike
India's lightning-prone states — Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, UP most affected; pre-monsoon season (April–June) has highest frequency; lightning kills 2000–2500 people annually in India

Damini app and lightning forecasting — IMD's Damini app provides real-time lightning alerts; Lightning Resilient India Campaign (LRIC); Integrated Lightning Protection System recommended for buildings
GLOF mechanism — glacial lakes (moraine-dammed, ice-dammed, bedrock) breach suddenly releasing stored water; NOT a snowslide or avalanche; Himalayas and Andes most affected globally
GLOF-prone regions in India — Uttarakhand (Chamoli GLOF 2021), Sikkim (South Lhonak Lake GLOF 2023), Himachal Pradesh; inventory by GSI and ISRO; 4,000+ glacial lakes in Indian Himalayas
Avalanche types — loose-snow (point release), slab (cohesive mass), wet (dense, slow), powder (fast, airblast); slab avalanches are most dangerous to humans
Snow avalanche hazard zones in India — J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand; SASE (Snow and Avalanche Study Establishment) under DRDO provides avalanche forecasting
Glacial retreat and GLOF risk — climate change accelerating glacial melt creates new glacial lakes; increasing GLOF frequency; linked to upstream infrastructure vulnerability (hydropower dams)
Cloudburst definition — IMD defines cloudburst as rainfall ≥100 mm/hour over a small area (~10 km² or less); very localized, intense convective precipitation; common in mountainous terrain
Orographic enhancement of cloudbursts — moisture-laden winds forced up mountain slopes cool adiabatically, condensing rapidly; Himalayan foothills and Western Ghats particularly prone

Flash flood vs riverine flood — flash flood onset within 6 hours of rainfall, high velocity, short duration; riverine flood slow onset (days to weeks), sustained duration; different warning and response timescales

Kedarnath 2013 disaster — cloudburst on Chorabari Lake combined with extreme rainfall caused catastrophic debris flow; >5000 deaths; declared India's worst cloudburst event; led to revision of disaster preparedness in Himalayas

sub_concepts.topic: Urban flooding causes — impervious surfaces reduce infiltration, overwhelm stormwater drainage; encroachment on natural drainage channels, wetlands, and floodplains eliminates flood buffering capacity

Mumbai floods 2005 (944 mm in 24 hours) — highlighted urban drainage failure; Chennai floods 2015 (excess reservoir releases + extreme rainfall); Bengaluru 2022 — IT hub flooding due to lake encroachment
National Urban Flood Risk Mitigation Plan — emphasis on stormwater master plans, drainage GIS mapping, enforcement of floodplain zoning regulations, BWSSB and BBMP roles in Bengaluru
Sponge city concept — urban planning approach integrating permeable surfaces, green infrastructure, and wetland restoration to absorb excess rainfall; China's pilot programs; relevance to India

Classification under NDMA — biological disasters include epidemics/pandemics, pest attacks (locust swarms), invasive species outbreaks; classified as biological, NOT meteorological or natural geophysical disasters

Locust swarms (Desert Locust — Schistocerca gregaria) — triggered by sudden vegetation growth after rare desert rains (often El Niño related); one km² swarm eats same amount as 35,000 people daily; FAO leads international response

India's locust threat — Rajasthan-Gujarat border (Thar Desert zone) is primary breeding ground; Locust Warning Organisation (LWO) under Ministry of Agriculture; 2019–2020 invasion was worst in 25 years

Epidemic vs pandemic — epidemic is widespread occurrence of disease in a community/region above expected; pandemic is epidemic occurring worldwide across multiple countries simultaneously; WHO declares Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)

notes: All seismic zone data from BIS IS-1893 (Part 1) 2016 — India uses 4-zone classification (II, III, IV, V); Zone I was abolished.
IMD cyclone and heat wave thresholds are frequently tested — memorize exact values as UPSC tests threshold precision.
NDMA vs NDRF vs SDMA roles are a perennial trap; NDMA is policy body, NDRF is operational force, SDMA is state-level mirror of NDMA.
Sendai Framework targets and Hyogo Framework comparison appear in multi-statement questions; note: Sendai is non-binding.
GLOF events (Chamoli 2021, Sikkim 2023) are high CA-relevance; connect to glacial lake inventory and climate change.
Biological disasters (locust, epidemic) are classified separately from hydro-meteorological and geophysical disasters in NDMA framework.
Urban flooding links to Polity (municipal governance), Environment (wetland encroachment), and Economy (disaster losses); watch for CA triggers.
Lightning kills more people annually in India than cyclones or earthquakes — counterintuitive fact UPSC tests.
